title: Reel Three: Redman's show and the bandstand incident
summary: A visiting show with Don Redman fronting McKinney's Cotton Pickers came to the club, and Redman ordered a famous tipsy musician off the stand, which turned Brown against drinking.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x:
Interview With Lawrence Brown
by Patricia Willard
Reel Three

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5385
We were talking about the shows -- some of the stage shows that used to come to the club.

Yes. One of the stage shows I remember was a show that came out with Don Redman. And he was fronting McKinney's Cotton Pickers Band at that time. And on the floor -- the show was Broomfield and Greely, was a dance team from the East. And their show was on.

It was during this time that things began to happen with me. It was during this show that one of my peculiar attitudes, I will say, came about. One of the members of this band was a very, very famous person. And we all idolized him as a musician. And heretofore I had never had much experience with the antics of musicians, and so I hadn't paid too much attention.

But Don Redman was a very, very good musician, and he was rather strict. And one of his musicians, it happened to be one that we idolized, got a bit tipsy this night. And I will never forget, Don Redman came over to him and said in no certain terms, 'Get off my bandstand.' And we were all so taken aback to see this great person be lowrated to the extent of the leader telling him to get out, get off the bandstand, that it affected me the rest of my career.
And until this day I never have been a person to take a drink. I don't drink, I don't smoke. I have no habits. I

have no hobbies, even. And it was more or less the lessons that I became acquainted with along the road that has stuck with me and affected me to the extent that I began to realize that only -- you can succeed only if you dodge, or at least become very adept at being able to control these pitfalls. Because I've seen many, many things since I've been in music, and so many of them have happened to very, very good artists at a time when it affected their careers.
